newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: ANZ Bank predicts fall in inflation to 2.2 pct.
newsitem.headline: ANZ Bank predicts fall in inflation to 2.2 pct.

text.p: ANZ Bank on Monday predicted inflation would fall to 2.2 percent for the year to March 1997, and suggested monetary conditions may be tighter than needed.

In its Market Focus newsletter, ANZ predicted underlying inflation at 0.4 percent in the March quarter, reducing the annual rate to 2.2 percent from 2.4 percent in the December quarter. Headline inflation is expected to be 0.1 percent for the quarter, or 2.2 percent for the year to March.
The forecasts come just over a week before the figures for March quarter consumer price index on April 15.
ANZ said the difference between the headline and the underlying rates was due to the delayed impact of falls in mortgage interest rates announced late last year.
Similarly, WestpacTrust is forecasting underlying inflation in the March 1997 quarter of 0.4 percent, lowering the annual rate to 2.1 percent.
Westpac forecasts headline inflation to be flat in the March quarter, bringing the annual headline inflation rate down to 2.1 percent from 2.6 percent in the December quarter.
In March, the Reserve Bank forecast headline inflation to rise 0.1 percent in the March quarter, and underlying inflation to rise 0.5 percent.

ANZ said cost increases in the housing and construction sector, in polytechnic and university fees, and price rises in some food items were the main reasons for the rise in inflation in the March quarter.
Offsetting factors were tight trading conditions in the retail sector, the strong New Zealand dollar and weakness in a range of tradable sector prices.
Tight retail trading conditions may be forcing importers to pass a greater proportion of the exchange rate gain to consumers than they have done in the past, it said.

"A March-quarter CPI result in line with our expectations may provide much-needed reassurance to the financial markets that New Zealand is indeed on track to achieve lower inflation over the year," ANZ said.

"Regardless of the impact of increased government spending on the longer-term inflation outlook, it may cause the markets to question why monetary conditions are tighter than the Reserve Bank requires at this time."
This could lead to some easing in short-term interest rates and/or the Kiwi dollar.
ANZ estimates the housing group to have contributed about a third of the increase in underlying inflation in the March quarter, and the education-recreation group about a quarter.
